clue.text: A source of divided views on the bridge

definitions.text: A source of divided views on the bridge

parts.words: A source of divided views on the bridge
parts.note: the bridge is not a ship's but the bridge of the nose, where spectacles with split lenses sit

explanation.surface: Something on a ship's bridge causes disagreement among the officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' suggests a ship or a card table; it is the bridge of the nose, and the divided views are lenses split into near and far halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles whose lenses are split into two zones for near and distant sight give a divided view.

clue.text: Ban on articles about the Cloth

parts.note: to ban is to bar

indicators.note: the two articles stand on either side of the word the

parts.note: two indefinite articles, A and A
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prohibition is placed on press articles concerning the clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Cloth' reads as the clergy; here it is simply a fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Barathea is a fine woollen fabric with a broken rib weave, used for suits and uniforms.

clue.text: High-pitched instrument has been sounded

parts.note: a small shrill whistle-like pipe; 'has been' said aloud is 'has bean', and the name is also that of a kind of bean

explanation.surface: A shrill instrument has just been played.
explanation.walkthrough: The name belongs both to a small high-pitched pipe and to a small French haricot bean, so 'has been sounded' hints 'has bean' as heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fipple flute with a piercing high tone, related to the recorder, shares its name with a pale green bean.

clue.text: Trojan maiden spurns the mountain plant

indicators.note: rejecting the mountain means its letters are dropped from the maiden's name

parts.note: Cressida, the Trojan heroine of Troilus and Cressida
Mount Ida, near Troy

explanation.surface: A young woman of Troy turns her back on an alpine flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountain plant' looks like one phrase for the definition; 'the mountain' is Ida, taken from CRESSIDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Watercress and garden cress are small pungent salad plants of the mustard family.

clue.text: Cement round catch in semicircular window

indicators.note: the cement word goes around the catch word

parts.note: lute is a clay or paste cement used to seal joints
to net is to catch

explanation.surface: Mortar is applied around a latch on an arched window.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunette is a crescent or half-moon shaped opening or window above a door or in a vault.

clue.text: Peg ratio in reverse gear

indicators.note: the ratio sits within the turned clothes word
the clothes word is written backwards

parts.note: togs are clothes, gear
pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter

explanation.surface: A mechanical ratio is shown with a car in reverse gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse gear' reads as motoring, but 'gear' means clothes and 'reverse' turns that word backwards to make SGOT; 'ratio' is the circle constant.
explanation.definitionFit: A spigot is a peg or plug used to stop the vent hole of a cask.

clue.text: Stage parts for the avant-garde?

parts.note: parts of a theatre stage lying in front of the scenery, the Latin and Greek 'pro' meaning before

explanation.surface: Roles in a play are written for experimental theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avant-garde' suggests experimental art; literally it means the part in front, and the stage areas in front of the scenery are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the forestage areas of theatres, in front of the curtain and its arch.

clue.text: Core about right for the size of rope

indicators.note: the core word goes around the letter for right

parts.note: the gist is the core of a matter

explanation.surface: The heart of the matter concerns the correct thickness of a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Grist is a ropemaker's term for a rope's thickness, its gauge in yarns.

clue.text: Very slight irritation, but extremely touchy about it

indicators.note: those two letters go around the irritation
the extremes of the word touchy are its first and last letters

parts.note: an itch is an irritation

explanation.surface: A minor annoyance, but someone gets very touchy about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Titchy is British slang for tiny or minute.

clue.text: Lucky like the face of a hag is, said Burns

definitions.text: like the face of a hag is, said Burns

explanation.surface: Burns remarks that a crone's face brings good fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns, in his poem To a Haggis, greets its 'honest, sonsie face'; 'hag is' is meant to be heard as haggis, the Scottish pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots word means both lucky or bringing good fortune and plump or comely, as Burns used it of the haggis's face.

clue.text: Study English author

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it

explanation.surface: Read up on an English writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade (1814-1884) was an English novelist and dramatist.

clue.text: His work has not been previously published

definitions.text: His work has not been previously published

parts.words: His work has not been previously published
parts.note: the work is not an unpublished book but new words, coined for the first time

explanation.surface: An author whose writing has never appeared in print.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue suggests an unpublished writer; what has never been published before is the person's coinages, words newly minted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who invents new words produces terms nobody has used in print before.

clue.text: Scurrilous officer, seen in all the right places

parts.note: taken as written
sites are places

explanation.surface: A foul-mouthed officer is spotted in all the fashionable haunts.
explanation.walkthrough: Thersites is the railing, abusive Greek of the Iliad and of Troilus and Cressida; 'officer' casts him loosely as one of the Greek army.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer and Shakespeare he is the foul-tongued Greek who abuses his commanders at Troy.

clue.text: You can't escape if this matrimonial prospect is 22!

definitions.text: You can't escape if this matrimonial prospect is 22!

parts.words: You can't escape if this matrimonial prospect is 22!
parts.note: a desirable marriage partner is a good one of these, and with the number 22 after it it names Heller's no-way-out dilemma

explanation.surface: An eligible partner of twenty-two leaves you no way out.
explanation.walkthrough: The '22' looks like a cross-reference or an age; it completes Joseph Heller's phrase for a dilemma with no escape, Catch-22.
explanation.definitionFit: A good marriage prospect is called a good catch, and a Catch-22 is a trap with no way out.

clue.text: Blow up General

annotationWithheld.why: 'Blow up General' (7): GENERAL rearranged gives the answer, but 'Blow up' must be both the definition and the anagram signal, one phrase doing two jobs.

clue.text: Brutus's noblest feature?

parts.note: Brutus was 'the noblest Roman of them all', so his facial feature is a Roman one, the aquiline kind

explanation.surface: What was the finest quality of Brutus?
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony calls Brutus 'the noblest Roman of them all' in Julius Caesar; the feature is facial, and a high-bridged one is called Roman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose has a prominent high bridge, and Brutus was a Roman with a noble profile.

clue.text: Not the father-figure in Terence's play, surely?

definitions.text: Not the father-figure in Terence's play, surely?

parts.words: Not the father-figure in Terence's play, surely?
parts.note: the title character of one of Terence's Roman comedies is a castrated man, who can hardly be anyone's father

explanation.surface: Surely the father is not the character in this Roman comedy?
explanation.walkthrough: Terence, the Roman comic playwright, named a play after a castrated character, so the title role can be no father-figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A castrated man, unable to father children, is the title figure of Terence's comedy.

clue.text: Country where, say, it's all part of the service

definitions.text: it's all part of the service

parts.note: China is a country

indicators.note: say tells us the next word is to be taken as heard

parts.note: the word where, spoken, gives a different spelling

explanation.surface: A country where, supposedly, everything is included in the service charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of the service' suggests a restaurant bill; it is a dinner service, all of which is porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Plates, cups and dishes of a dinner service are made of porcelain.

clue.text: He has a slide to play with in the pit

definitions.text: He has a slide to play with in the pit

parts.words: He has a slide to play with in the pit
parts.note: the pit is the orchestra pit, and the slide is the moving tube of a brass instrument

explanation.surface: A child in a sandpit or playground has a slide to amuse himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slide' and 'pit' suggest a playground or a mine; the pit is the orchestra pit and the slide is the instrument's sliding tube.
explanation.definitionFit: This brass instrument changes pitch with a sliding tube and is played in theatre orchestras.

clue.text: Fertiliser made from aments

indicators.note: the answer is built by rearranging the letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Plant feed is manufactured from catkins.
explanation.walkthrough: Aments are catkins, so the surface is botanical throughout; 'fertiliser' means the pollen-bearing male organ of a flower, not plant food.
explanation.definitionFit: The pollen-producing male organ of a flower fertilises the ovule.

clue.text: New offence about which old king is moving cautiously

indicators.note: the old king's name is placed around the offence

parts.note: Og was the Old Testament king of Bashan
a sin is an offence

explanation.surface: A fresh crime around which an elderly monarch creeps carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Og, king of Bashan in the Bible, is a crossword stock king; it splits around SIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Edging forward warily, nose first, is a cautious way of moving.

clue.text: Artisan's portable heater

explanation.surface: A craftsman's movable stove.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Artisan's' merely joins the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker in brass is one sense; the other is a metal pan or stand holding burning coals for warmth.

clue.text: Dispenser — the sort that sucks up

definitions.text: Dispenser — the sort that sucks up

parts.words: Dispenser — the sort that sucks up
parts.note: a graduated glass tube that delivers measured liquid in the laboratory, filled by drawing the liquid up into it

explanation.surface: A dispensing machine of the kind that absorbs its contents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucks up' suggests a toady; it is literal, a lab tube filled by drawing liquid up.
explanation.definitionFit: A graduated glass tube with a tap, used in titration to release precise volumes of liquid.

clue.text: Ignominious result of contribution to the Mafia's Cosa Nostra

indicators.note: the letters come from a stretch of the words that follow, a part of their whole

explanation.surface: The shameful outcome of a donation to the Mafia.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiasco is a complete and humiliating failure.

clue.text: Really honest, this poor Hindu

parts.note: 'honest' plus this word is an old slang oath meaning truly, and the word itself is a corruption of the word for a native of India

explanation.surface: A poor Indian swears he is telling the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honest Injun!' is old slang for 'truly'; the word is a debased form of 'Indian', which the clue loosely renders 'poor Hindu'.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang oath 'honest Injun' means truly, and the word is a corrupted spelling of Indian.

clue.text: Moves swiftly to dodge boisterous fun

explanation.surface: Someone dodges quickly to escape the horseplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High jinks' is the phrase for boisterous fun.
explanation.definitionFit: To dart sideways evading a tackle is one sense; the other is lively, rowdy merrymaking.

clue.text: Telling a member to use force

parts.note: a telling argument is a strong one
an arm is a limb or member

explanation.surface: Telling someone in a club to resort to violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club member; it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong-arm tactics are those that bully with physical force.

clue.text: Northern song about many in the pits.

indicators.note: the song word goes around the letter for many

parts.note: an air is a song
D is the Roman numeral for 500, many

explanation.surface: A northern song about the many miners down the pits.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests coal mining; 'the pits' is slang for the lowest point.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point, which 'the pits' means colloquially.

clue.text: Apollo has engine cover as heat shield

parts.note: Apollo was the Greek god of the sun
a car's bonnet covers its engine

explanation.surface: An Apollo spacecraft has a protective cover against re-entry heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apollo' and 'heat shield' suggest space missions; the shield is a hat against the sun. BONNET is the British word for a car's hood.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide-brimmed hat protects the wearer from the sun's heat.

clue.text: Legislator has to take action about motorists

indicators.note: the action word goes around the motoring club

parts.note: to do is to take action
the RAC (Royal Automobile Club) is a British motoring organisation

explanation.surface: A lawmaker must act on behalf of drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: Draco was the Athenian lawgiver whose harsh code gave us 'draconian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco drew up the first written law code of Athens, famously severe.

clue.text: Drunk used to being ejected

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters reel about into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunk is accustomed to being thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ousted has been forced out or expelled.

clue.text: Theatre Royal, one day before getting new lease of life

parts.note: rep is short for repertory theatre
I is the Roman numeral one
the eve is the day before

explanation.surface: The Theatre Royal, on the eve of closure, is given a fresh start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre Royal' reads as one name; it is two pieces, REP and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay of execution or cancellation gives a fresh lease of life.
